item.title: Mount Ishizuchi: Western Japan's Highest Peak — Guide
item.description: Mount Ishizuchi, rising to 1,982 metres, is the highest mountain in western Japan and one of the country’s seven great sacred peaks, revered for centuries as a place of mountain worship and ascetic training. Reaching the summit is a genuine mountain hike, made famous — and thrilling — by its kusari, heavy iron chains bolted to sheer rock faces that climbers haul themselves up, testing nerve and strength (bypass trails exist for those who prefer).

item.title: Mount Tsurugi: Shikoku's Second Peak — Guide
item.description: Mount Tsurugi (Tsurugi-san), rising to 1,955 metres above the Iya Valley, is the second-highest peak in Shikoku and one of Japan’s revered sacred mountains, long a site of mountain worship. Unusually for such a high peak, it is remarkably accessible: a chairlift carries you much of the way up, from where a well-marked trail of around 40 minutes leads to the summit. In contrast to its rocky lower slopes, the top is a broad, gentle ridge covered in grass and low bamboo, laid with boardwalks to protect the alpine plants, opening to sweeping 360-degree panoramas over range after range of Shikoku’s mountains.

item.title: Omiwa Shrine: Japan's Oldest Shrine and Its Sacred Mountain — Guide
item.description: Omiwa Shrine (Oomiwa) near Sakurai is often called the oldest shrine in Japan, and it preserves the most ancient form of Shinto worship: it has no honden, no main sanctuary building, because the object of worship is Mount Miwa itself, the sacred conical mountain rising behind it, revered as the dwelling of the deity since before recorded history. Worshippers pray at a hall facing the mountain, passing beneath one of Japan’s largest torii gates.

item.title: Hakusan National Park: One of Japan's Three Sacred Mountains — Guide
item.description: Mount Hakusan has been venerated as one of Japan’s three sacred mountains, alongside Fuji and Tateyama, for over a thousand years, worshipped as a source of water and fertility by farming communities across the surrounding region, and remains an active pilgrimage site today. The national park surrounding the mountain offers alpine hiking trails ranging from accessible day walks to more demanding multi-day routes to the 2,702-metre summit, passing wildflower meadows, volcanic crater lakes and dramatic mountain scenery that draws hikers throughout the warmer months.

item.title: Mt. Gassan: Summer Skiing Among Wildflowers — Guide
item.description: Gassan, the central peak of the Dewa Sanzan, has Japan’s longest alpine ski season — snow covers the upper slopes from November through late July, making June and July skiing among flowers a uniquely Japanese experience. As the ski season finally yields to summer, the mountain erupts with alpine wildflowers including snow buttercups, Japanese primrose and carpets of hanazo across the high plateau. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Haguro/Nishikawa, Yamagata Hours Ski season ~Apr–Jul Admission Lift/gondola fees apply Time needed Half day–full day Best time June–July (skiing + wildflowers) What to Do Ski or snowboard into late July — Japan’s longest season.

item.title: Mt. Hayachine: Iwate's Sacred Alpine-Flower Peak — Guide
item.description: Mt. Hayachine (1,917 m) is Iwate’s most sacred mountain — a rugged serpentine-rock massif supporting rare endemic alpine plants found nowhere else on earth. In July and August the summit plateau is carpeted in Hayachine usuyukiso (a unique alpine edelweiss relative), drawing botanists and hikers from across Japan. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hanamaki/Tono border, Iwate Hours Hiking season ~Jun–Oct Admission Free Time needed Full day (summit hike) Best time Jul–Aug (alpine flowers) What to See Rare endemic alpine flowers (Hayachine usuyukiso).

item.title: Osorezan (Mt. Fear): Japan's Gate to the Afterlife — Guide
item.description: Osorezan, or ‘Mount Fear’, is one of Japan’s three most sacred sites — a bleak volcanic caldera on the remote Shimokita Peninsula. Sulfur fumes, grey pumice fields and a startlingly blue crater lake create a landscape Buddhists have long seen as the very entrance to the afterlife. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Mutsu City, Shimokita, Aomori Hours ~6:00–18:00, May–Oct Admission Around ¥500 Time needed 1.

item.title: Toyama Power Spots: Tateyama's Mountain Deity, Zuiryuji's Zen Energy & Gokayama's Secret Valley
item.description: Toyama’s spiritual geography is anchored by one of Japan’s three sacred mountains — a peak that medieval Buddhist cosmology mapped as the actual entrance to the afterlife — and a Rinzai Zen temple whose geometric perfection has been drawing visitors to stillness for nearly 400 years. Between these two poles, the deep mountain isolation of Gokayama and the volcanic fumaroles of the Tateyama caldera contribute to a landscape that accumulates spiritual resonance in ways that are felt even by secular visitors.
